newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sources see special funds probe as inevitable.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sources see special funds probe as inevitable.

text.p: Pressure is building on Attorney General Janet Reno for an independent investigation into the Democratic fund-raising controversy, and even some of her own officials concede such a probe is "inevitable."

So far Reno has refused to seek the appointment of an independent counsel to take over the investigation into the fund-raising allegations that have dogged the White House, insisting there was no legal reason for her to act.

Two Justice Department officials privately questioned Reno's judgment, calling an independent counsel "inevitable" and criticising her for interpreting the law very narrowly in deciding so far against an outside probe.

But others in the Justice Department disagreed with the assessment that Reno must act, saying that was not credible evidence that any White House official broke the law in their zeal to raise millions of dollars for the 1996 campaign.
Under U.S. law, Reno alone must decide whether to trigger the process that would lead to a special prosecutor.

Reno's position has provided welcome relief to the White House, where officials want to avoid another long, costly probe similar to the one Whitewater special prosecutor Kenneth Starr has conducted involving President Clinton and the first lady.
Starr has been investigating the failed Whitewater land deal in which the Clintons and some friends invested when he was governor of Arkansas.

"The White House is concerned that a rabid partisan (Republican) will be appointed, that people will run up big legal bills and it will never end for the next four years," said one administration official.
At a news conference on Friday, Clinton rejected suggestions that he should call for an independent counsel.

"It is a legal question. I do not think it should become a political question. And I have been very rigorous in dealing with this and saying it just that way, and I'm going to stick with my position," he said.
But Republican leaders in Congress are doing all they can to force Reno to act.

The Republican-controlled Senate Judiciary Committee has scheduled a vote on Thursday on a resolution demanding that Reno at least open a preliminary investigation under the independent counsel law or report in writing why she refused.

"I think that the threshold for triggering the appointment of an independent counsel has been met," Sen. Orrin Hatch, the committee chairman and a Utah Republican, said, adding that an outside probe seemed "inescapable."

On CNN's "Inside Politics" on Saturday, he said, "When you add it all up, there seems to be specific and credible evidence enough," citing an apparent "conflict of interest because of the high level involvement in the White House."

Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, a New York Democrat who has publicly called for an independent probe, said Saturday he found reports about fundraising activities by Taiwanese-American entrepeneur Johnny Chung "disturbing."
Chung donated over $350,000 to the Democratic Party, but most of the money was returned because its origin was unclear.

"I think there is an attack on our system from Asia, from Indonesia and mainland China, and as well as perhaps from Taiwan," Moynihan told CNN's "Evans & Novak." "The system was attacked and some of it was penetrated."

Just before Clinton decided to keep Reno in his Cabinet during his second term in office, White House aides voiced displeasure that she too often had sought independent counsel probes into other administration controversies.
"I guess Ms. Reno is being conservative because she got flack about prior recommendations for independent counsels," one Justice Department official said.

The official said the case for an independent counsel was bolstered after last week's disclosures that Vice President Al Gore solicited campaign funds by telephone from his White House office and that Maggie Williams, Hillary Rodham Clinton's top aide, accepted a $50,000 political donation from Chung.
If Reno resists an independent counsel, the allegations will continue to be investigated by a Justice Department task force led by prosecutors from its public integrity section.
The task force will soon add six more FBI agents to the 25 already working on the investigation. It has issued subpoenas and has called witnesses before a federal grand jury.
